policies.summary: Counties and municipalities decide siting of wind and solar; state land use review by the Office of State Planning Coordination is advisory and the local jurisdiction keeps final decision-making authority. A separate statute bars local rules stricter than set limits only for residential wind systems, not utility-scale projects.

restrictions.description: New Castle County's Unified Development Code (Sec. 40.03.337) requires large-scale solar energy systems to sit at least 50 feet from any property line and 150 feet from any dwelling, caps total solar in the Suburban Reserve district at 1,000 acres, bars solar on conservation or preservation easements that are publicly funded or government-required to the extent it would materially interfere with the easement, and keeps solar 660 feet from designated byways.
restrictions.long_description: setback: 50 ft from any property line, 150 ft from any dwelling unit; cap on area: total aggregate acres of all SES uses in the SR district not to exceed 1,000, and up to 85 percent of site acreage in SR and S; zoning restriction: large-scale SES prohibited (N) in TN, ST, CN, SE, NC, EX and P districts (Table 40.03.110), limited use review elsewhere, and not allowed on land under a conservation or preservation easement acquired with public funds or required by a government entity, to the extent the SES would materially interfere with any purpose of the easement; visual_impact_rule: not within 660 ft of a designated byway right-of-way (200 ft for community solar outside SR in the Coastal Zone)

rows.mechanisms: setback, cap on area, zoning restriction, visual_impact_rule

restrictions.description: In March 2022, the Kent County Levy Court imposed a moratorium on new solar projects in response to pushback after allowing solar projects to be sited on agricultural lands.
restrictions.long_description: In March 2022, the Kent County Levy Court imposed a moratorium on new solar projects in response to pushback after allowing solar projects to be sited on agricultural lands. In September 2022, the Levy Court amended the County ordinance to prohibit new solar farms larger than 50 acres on agricultural land, thereby reducing the potential available land from 75,000 acres to 1,500 acres, a reduction of approximately 98%.

projects.description: In March 2022, a landowner in Smyrna and a group called Citizens Against Solar Pollution filed a lawsuit in Delaware Chancery Court challenging Kent County’s approval of the proposed 100-MW Cedar Creek Solar project on agricultural land.
projects.long_description: In March 2022, a landowner in Smyrna and a group called Citizens Against Solar Pollution filed a lawsuit in Delaware Chancery Court challenging Kent County’s approval of the proposed 100-MW Cedar Creek Solar project on agricultural land. The lawsuit alleged that the project would damage the environment, reduce property values, disrupt the rural character of the community, and threaten historical artifacts.

projects.description: In May 2024, the Frankford Town Council voted to deny an application for a 44-acre solar farm proposed by Dukes Farm Limited Partnership, after the town’s Planning & Zoning Committee recommended the application’s denial.
projects.long_description: In May 2024, the Frankford Town Council voted to deny an application for a 44-acre solar farm proposed by Dukes Farm Limited Partnership, after the town’s Planning & Zoning Committee recommended the application’s denial. The decision came after a public meeting at which local residents expressed reservations about the project. The application was denied because it did not meet certain criteria in the town’s 2020 Comprehensive Plan, such as criteria for maintaining a “small-town feel.”

projects.project_name: Skipjack Wind Farm Interconnection Facility in Fenwick State Park
projects.description: The Skipjack Wind Farm, a proposed offshore wind project near Ocean City, was originally planned to connect to the grid at a facility in Delaware’s Fenwick Island State Park.
projects.long_description: The Skipjack Wind Farm, a proposed offshore wind project near Ocean City, was originally planned to connect to the grid at a facility in Delaware’s Fenwick Island State Park. The plan received pushback from the Delaware Chapter of the Surfrider Foundation, who argued that the plan to install transmission infrastructure in a state park was contrary to the mission of the Delaware Division of Parks and Recreation. In 2020, the developer abandoned plans to site the interconnection facility at Fenwick Island State Park.

projects.description: A Lewes resident filed two lawsuits in state and federal court to halt the operation of a wind turbine used for research by the University of Delaware, arguing that backroom dealings led to an expedited approval process.
projects.long_description: A Lewes resident filed two lawsuits in state and federal court to halt the operation of a wind turbine used for research by the University of Delaware, arguing that backroom dealings led to an expedited approval process. The federal lawsuit was dismissed in January 2015. In the state lawsuit, the Delaware Court of Chancery granted summary judgment against the plaintiff on multiple claims in December 2015, which the Delaware Supreme Court affirmed in August 2016.

projects.description: In July 2024, the Sussex County Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended approval of Renewable Redevelopment’s application for a conditional use permit to build a substation in Dagsboro to support US Wind’s offshore wind project.
projects.long_description: In July 2024, the Sussex County Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended approval of Renewable Redevelopment’s application for a conditional use permit to build a substation in Dagsboro to support US Wind’s offshore wind project. The offshore wind project consists of 121 wind turbines and up to four offshore substations. In December 2024, the Sussex County Council, in a 4-1 vote, denied a conditional use permit for the Dagsboro substation citing lack of direct benefits to the residents of Sussex County among the reasons for denial. In June 2025, the state legislature enacted Senate Bill 159, which requires the permitting of an electric substation as an allowed conditional use in a heavy industrial zone under certain conditions, including to support the operation of a renewable energy project of 250 MW or more. The state law was given retroactive effect to August 3, 2023. The law overrides the council’s denial of the project. Sussex County and the Town of Fenwick Island, the municipalities involved in the US Wind project, challenged the law in the Delaware Court of Chancery. In March 2026, the Delaware Court of Chancery upheld the General Assembly’s authority to override Sussex County Council’s denial. In May 2026, the Delaware Supreme Court affirmed the decision by the Court of Chancery upholding the state law and overturning the Council’s denial of the conditional use permit for the Dagsboro substation.
